subtype: Approach: asks how to make a situation worse to spot hidden levers [Thinking]
passage: Kashish, you say your meetings are chaos, so here's a trick from my own team. I'm Charu. Our meetings ran long and loud, and everyone complained but nobody knew where to start. So one Friday I asked the room, 'How would we make these meetings even worse?' People laughed, then answered fast: send the agenda five minutes before, and never write anything down, so we can argue later about what we agreed. Somebody said, 'We already do both.' That stopped us. We changed only those two things: agendas the evening before, and one person taking notes and sending them the same day. Within a month the meetings were forty minutes instead of an hour and a half, and the shouting faded. I still ask the 'worse' question when I'm stuck.

qa.q: How long were the meetings after a month?
qa.a: After a month the meetings were forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling before asking the 'worse' question?
qa.a: Charu was stuck and probably frustrated, since everyone complained but nobody knew where to start.

qa.q: Which turning point made the hidden causes visible?
qa.a: Asking how to make the meetings worse and hearing 'We already do both' showed the causes, so two simple changes could be made.

qa.q: How might the team have felt when somebody said 'We already do both'?
qa.a: The team was probably struck by the truth in it, maybe a little embarrassed, since it stopped them.

grounding: Shows a manager asking what would make noisy meetings worse, spotting late agendas and no notes as hidden levers, and fixing those two.

Mridul had inherited the weekly project meeting along with the team, and it was a mess: ninety minutes, everyone talking over each other, nobody sure what was decided. This week there was an extra problem. Half the team was on a shaky video link from the Nagpur site, and the other half was in a small room where the air conditioner roared.
Before the next meeting, Mridul tried a strange question on a notepad: how could I make this meeting even worse?
Send the agenda five minutes before. Take no notes. Let the loudest person go first. Leave the site team on mute until the end.
He looked at the first two. Those were already true.
So on Monday, the agenda went out on Friday afternoon. Vaibhav agreed to take notes on a shared screen. The meeting ended in forty minutes, and for once the site team spoke without shouting.
"Short," Vaibhav said afterwards. "And we know what we decided."

qa.q: How long did Monday's meeting take?
qa.a: The meeting ended in forty minutes.

qa.q: How did Mridul feel on noticing the first two items were already true?
qa.a: He felt a jolt of recognition and some embarrassment, seeing that his meeting already did the worst things on the list.

qa.q: What else could Mridul fix using the same list, and why?
qa.a: He could give the site team the first turn to speak, since leaving them till the end was another way to make the meeting worse.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see the new meeting?
qa.a: Vaibhav is relieved and pleased that it was short and that everyone knows what was decided.

grounding: It shows a manager asking what would make a noisy meeting culture worse, noticing late agendas and no notes, and fixing those two to make meetings shorter and calmer.

Vaibhav's team meetings in the Gurugram office were famous for the wrong reasons. People brought laptops and answered emails. Discussions looped. Nobody left knowing who was doing what.
On Sunday evening, he tried flipping the question. Not how to fix it, but how to make it even worse.
He wrote: share the agenda at the door. Don't write anything down. Invite everyone even if their topic isn't on it. Let it run as long as it likes.
Two of those made him wince. Agendas came late, often in the meeting itself. Notes were never taken, so Imran and others asked the same questions every week.
He changed only those two. Agenda by Thursday evening, and a rotating note-taker with a shared page.
Three weeks later, Imran stopped him in the corridor. "Meetings are half as long. And calm. What happened?"
"I made a list of how to make them worse," Vaibhav said, smiling.

qa.q: What day did Vaibhav start sending the agenda?
How did Vaibhav feel when two items on his list made him wince?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and a bit embarrassed, seeing his own meetings already did those two things.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav try if meetings still ran long?
qa.a: He could end each topic with a named owner and a date, since people leaving without knowing who does what was the other problem.

qa.q: How does Imran experience the new meetings?
qa.a: Imran is pleasantly surprised that meetings are half as long and calm, and curious enough to ask what changed.

grounding: It shows a manager asking what would make meetings worse, finding late agendas and no notes, and fixing those two for shorter, calmer meetings.
